what_its_for: Sulindac is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to relieve pain, swelling, stiffness, and tenderness caused by arthritis (including osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis), gout attacks, and bursitis or tendinitis.
how_to_take: Take sulindac by mouth with a full glass of water (8 ounces). Always take it with food, milk, or antacids to help protect your stomach. Do not lie down for at least 10 minutes after taking this medicine. Swallow the tablet whole or you may crush it and mix with food or water if needed. Take it at the same times each day to keep a steady amount in your body.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 150 mg to 200 mg taken twice a day (every 12 hours). Your doctor will adjust the dose based on your condition. Do not take more than 400 mg in one day unless your doctor tells you to. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store sulindac at room temperature between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, direct light, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use medicine past the expiration date on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking sulindac, as it increases your risk of stomach bleeding. Do not take aspirin or other NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen or naproxen) at the same time unless your doctor approves. Avoid smoking, as it can also worsen stomach problems. Be careful with activities that require alertness if you feel dizzy. Tell your doctor before using any blood thinners, steroids, or heart medications.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice: black, tarry, or bloody stools; vomit that looks like coffee grounds; chest pain, shortness of breath, or sudden weakness (possible signs of a heart attack or stroke); swelling in your legs or feet; sudden weight gain; yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); severe stomach pain; skin rash, blistering, or peeling; or decreased or no urination. Also call if your pain gets worse or you do not feel better after a few days.
when_it_works: Sulindac may begin to relieve pain and reduce swelling within a few hours to a few days of starting treatment. However, for long-term conditions like arthritis, it may take 1 to 2 weeks of regular use before you feel the full benefit. Keep taking it as directed even if you feel better.
special_populations: Older adults (age 65 and older) are at higher risk for stomach bleeding and kidney problems with this medicine — use the lowest effective dose and report any unusual symptoms to your doctor promptly. Pregnant women should avoid sulindac, especially in the last 3 months of pregnancy, as it can harm the unborn baby. Tell your doctor if you are breastfeeding before taking this medicine. Children: safety and dosing in children have not been well established — use only if directed by a doctor. Patients with kidney disease, liver disease, heart disease, high blood pressure, or a history of stomach ulcers should use this medicine with extra caution and close medical supervision.
